        2. analyse the contents of the repo and create following.
            2.1 create/update dockerfile based on the analysis.

function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: Generates a Dockerfile in the specified repository directory with a default configuration. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the repository directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory name within the filesystem.

base_image.description: The base image to use in the Dockerfile. For example, 'python:3.8-slim'.

maintainer.description: The maintainer information to be added to the Dockerfile. Format should be 'Name <email@example.com>'.

port.description: The port number that the container will expose. For example, '80' for a web server.

commands.description: Additional commands to be executed when building the image, separated by ';'. For example, 'apt-get update; apt-get install -y git'.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be a valid path relative to the project root.

deployment_name.description: The name to assign to the Kubernetes deployment. This name must be unique within the Kubernetes namespace.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to use for the deployment. This should include the repository name and tag, if applicable, in the format 'repository/image:tag'.

replicas.description: The number of instances to deploy for the specified Docker image.

service_type.description: The type of service to create for the deployment. Typical values include 'ClusterIP', 'NodePort', and 'LoadBalancer'.

port.description: The port number that the service should expose. This should correspond to the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

target_port.description: The target port on the pod to which the service will send requests. This should be the same as the port that the application inside the Docker container is set to listen on.

function.name: analyse_repo_contents
function.description: Analyzes the contents of a repository to determine the predominant programming language used within. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the repository is located. This should be the root directory of the repository.

include_subdirectories.description: A flag indicating whether to include subdirectories in the analysis. If set to true, all subdirectories will be recursively analyzed.

excluded_files.description: An array of file names or patterns to exclude from the analysis, such as ['README.md', '*.txt'].

language_threshold.description: The percentage threshold for a language to be considered predominant in the repository. This should be a value between 0 and 100. This is a float type value.

message.content:
Below is a practical “recipe” you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or adapt to your CI/CD pipeline) to accomplish everything you asked for.  
I’ll walk through each numbered step, give you the exact shell commands, and show the minimal code that the helper functions would generate.  

> **NOTE** – I don’t have direct access to your machine or to the internet, so I can’t actually clone the repo or push the changes for you.  
> What follows is a *complete* set of instructions you can run locally (or in a CI job) to get the desired outcome.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# Make sure you have SSH keys set up for GitHub
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

If you prefer HTTPS:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repository & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Detect the dominant language

```bash
# Using the helper function (pseudo‑code)
result = functions.analyse_repo_contents({
    "directory_name": ".",
    "include_subdirectories": True,
    "excluded_files": ["README.md"],
    "language_threshold": 10.0
})
print(result)
```

> In practice this will return something like `{"predominant_language":"JavaScript","percentage":95.3}`.  
> For a typical Node.js repo you’ll see JavaScript (or TypeScript) dominate.

### 2.2 Create / update the Dockerfile

```bash
# Call the helper function (pseudo‑code)
docker_result = functions.create_a_docker_file({
    "directory_name": ".",          # current repo root
    "base_image": "node:18-alpine", # lightweight Node runtime
    "maintainer": "Your Name <you@example.com>",
    "port": 3000,                   # adjust to your app’s listening port
    "commands": ""                  # no extra build steps needed
})
print(docker_result)
```

> The function will write a file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root with contents similar to:

```Dockerfile
# Generated by create_a_docker_file
FROM node:18-alpine
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAMLs

```bash
k8s_result = functions.create_kubernetes_yaml_file({
    "directory_name": ".",              # repo root
    "deployment_name": "nodejs-welcome",
    "image_name": "your-docker-registry/nodejs-welcome:latest",
    "replicas": 3,
    "service_type": "ClusterIP",
    "port": 80,
    "target_port": 3000
})
print(k8s_result)
```

> The function will create a file called `k8s.yaml` containing both Deployment and Service definitions:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: your-docker-registry/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> Replace `your-docker-registry` with whatever registry you’re using (e.g., `ghcr.io/zelarhq`).

### 2.4 Add a GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/build.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write   # required for ghcr.io
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Important:**  
> • Ensure the repository has the `GITHUB_TOKEN` secret (it does automatically).  
> • If you’re using another registry (e.g., Docker Hub), replace the login and tags accordingly.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new/updated files

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/build.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will trigger automatically on the next push to `main`.  
> You’ll see the “Build & Push Docker Image” job run in the Actions tab, and the image will appear in your registry.

---

## Quick sanity check

Once the workflow finishes, verify the image exists:

```bash
docker pull ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
docker run -d -p 8080:3000 ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
curl http://localhost:8080
```

You should receive the expected response from your Node.js app.

---

### Recap of what was generated

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a production image for the Node.js app |
| `k8s.yaml` | Deploys the app to Kubernetes (Deployment + Service) |
| `.github/workflows/build.yml` | Automates Docker build & push on pushes to `main` |

Feel free to tweak the parameters (image tags, replica count, service type, etc.) to suit your environment. Happy coding!
